title: The repair café
situation_ru: Ведущий радио берёт интервью у женщины, которая организовала бесплатное кафе починки вещей.
script:
Presenter: My guest today is Helen Price, who started a repair café in her local community centre three years ago. Helen, what exactly is a repair café?
Helen: Basically, it's a free event where people bring things that are broken, like a lamp, a jacket with a broken zip or a bike that won't change gear, and volunteers help them fix it. The idea is that you learn how to do it yourself, rather than just leaving it with us.
Presenter: And why did you start it?
Helen: Honestly, it began out of frustration. My toaster stopped working, and the shop told me it would be cheaper to buy a new one than to repair it. That seemed absurd to me. I knew there must be people around who had the skills to fix things, and plenty of people who'd love to learn.
Presenter: Who are your volunteers?
Helen: All sorts. We've got a retired electrician, a couple of students who are brilliant with phones, and a woman in her eighties who can repair almost any piece of clothing. That mix is one of my favourite things about it. People who'd never normally meet end up chatting for hours.
Presenter: Does everything get fixed?
Helen: No, and I think it's important to be honest about that. Roughly two thirds of the items leave working. Some things are simply designed so they can't be opened. That's actually what frustrates me most: not the broken things, but the products that are made to be thrown away.
Presenter: What would you say to someone thinking of starting one?
Helen: Start small. We began with four volunteers and a borrowed table. You don't need money. You need a room, some tools and a bit of patience.

questions.q: What is the main aim of the repair café, according to Helen?
options: Teaching people to fix things themselves
Fixing items quickly so people can collect them later
Selling repaired items to raise money for the centre
Collecting broken things so they can be recycled
questions.explain_ru: «The idea is that you learn how to do it yourself, rather than just leaving it with us».

questions.q: What made Helen start the repair café?
options: Her local council asked her to organise it
A shop said a new toaster was cheaper than a repair
She wanted to sell second-hand things locally
She lost her job as an electrician and had free time
questions.explain_ru: Магазин сказал, что купить новый тостер дешевле, чем починить старый.

questions.q: What does Helen enjoy most about the volunteers?
options: They are all trained professionals with years of experience
They work very quickly
They bring together people who wouldn't usually meet
They fix every single item
questions.explain_ru: Ей нравится, что встречаются люди, которые иначе никогда бы не познакомились.

questions.q: Roughly what share of the items leave the café working?
options: About half
About two thirds
Nearly all of them
About a third
questions.explain_ru: «Roughly two thirds of the items leave working».

questions.q: What frustrates Helen most?
options: People who don't want to learn
Volunteers who don't turn up on time
Things people forget to collect afterwards
Products that are made to be thrown away
questions.explain_ru: Больше всего её раздражают вещи, которые сделаны, чтобы их выбрасывали.

questions.q: What is Helen's advice to someone starting a repair café?
options: Start small, because you don't need much money
Find a big sponsor before you begin anything
Only accept electrical items at the start
Train your volunteers for several months before you open
questions.explain_ru: Начинать с малого: нужны комната, инструменты и терпение, а не деньги.

situation_en: A radio presenter interviews a woman who started a free repair café.

topic_en: Podcast discussion: back to the office?
title: Work in Progress
situation_ru: Два ведущих подкаста о работе обсуждают удалённую и офисную работу.
script:
Jen: Welcome back to Work in Progress. Rob, this week's topic is one we've been arguing about for months: should companies bring everyone back to the office?
Rob: Well, I'll admit I've changed my mind on this. Two years ago I'd have said remote work was perfect. No commute, more time with the kids, fewer pointless meetings.
Jen: And now?
Rob: Now I think something got lost. When I started my career, I learned most of what I know by sitting next to people who were better than me, overhearing their phone calls and asking quick questions. I'm not sure young employees get that on a video call.
Jen: That's fair, but I'd push back a bit. For a lot of people, like parents, people with long commutes or people with health issues, remote work has made it possible to keep a career at all. Forcing everyone back five days a week feels like solving one problem by creating another.
Rob: Oh, I'm not suggesting five days. I just think the office should be for the things that really need people together: training, brainstorming, building relationships. The rest can happen anywhere.
Jen: So, basically, hybrid.
Rob: Hybrid, but planned properly. What doesn't work is when everyone comes in on different days and then spends the whole time on video calls anyway.
Jen: Ha, I've definitely done that. OK, so where do we agree? I think we both believe the real question isn't whether to work in the office or at home, but what each place is actually good for.
Rob: Exactly. And I'd add that companies should ask their staff, rather than just announcing a policy from the top.
Jen: Agreed. Let us know what your company is doing, and we'll read some of your messages next week.

questions.q: How has Rob's opinion changed?
options: He now thinks everyone should be back in the office every day
He's less enthusiastic about fully remote work than before
He has become much more positive about video calls
He hasn't really changed his mind at all
questions.explain_ru: Раньше Роб считал удалёнку идеальной, теперь видит в ней минусы.

questions.q: Why does Rob think young employees may lose out?
options: They miss chances to learn from colleagues
They usually earn less than older staff
They have the longest commutes
They attend too many pointless meetings
questions.explain_ru: Он сам учился, сидя рядом с опытными коллегами, а по видеосвязи так не выйдет.

questions.q: What worries Jen about bringing everyone back five days a week?
options: Offices have become far too expensive for most companies to run
Young employees prefer to work from cafés
Video calls would stop working properly
Some people might not be able to keep their jobs
questions.explain_ru: Для многих удалёнка — единственная возможность сохранить карьеру.

questions.q: According to Rob, what doesn't work in hybrid arrangements?
options: Having fixed office days for the whole team
Using the office mainly for training sessions
Going in only to spend the day on calls
Having meetings in person instead of online
questions.explain_ru: «Everyone comes in on different days and then spends the whole time on video calls anyway».

questions.q: What do Jen and Rob agree on?
options: Offices should close down completely and permanently
Everyone should work from home on Fridays and Mondays
Each place should be used for what it does best
Video calls are better than face-to-face meetings
questions.explain_ru: Вопрос не «офис или дом», а для чего лучше подходит каждое место.

questions.q: What does Rob think companies should do?
options: Copy what other companies are doing
Wait to see how hybrid work develops
Test any new policy in one team first
Ask their staff what they think
questions.explain_ru: «Companies should ask their staff, rather than just announcing a policy from the top».

situation_en: Two podcast hosts discuss working from home and working in an office.

topic_en: A couple discussing a move to the countryside
title: A house in the country
situation_ru: Пара обсуждает, не переехать ли из города в деревню.
script:
Mark: I saw another house online today. Three bedrooms, a big garden, twenty minutes from the sea. And it costs less than this flat.
Anna: Let me guess. It's in the middle of nowhere.
Mark: It's in a village. There's a shop, a pub, a primary school.
Anna: And the nearest train station?
Mark: Forty minutes by car. But I'd only have to go into the office once a week.
Anna: You would. I'd have to go in three days a week, remember? That's a lot of driving.
Mark: True, but the roads out there are quiet. It's not like sitting in city traffic for an hour.
Anna: Maybe. Still, that's almost an hour and a half a day.
Mark: I know, I know. But think about it. We'd have space. We could finally get a dog. And we wouldn't be breathing traffic fumes every time we open the window.
Anna: I'm not saying it's a bad idea. I grew up in a village, so I know how lovely it can be. I also know how quiet it gets in winter. When it's dark at four o'clock and all your friends are two hours away, the garden doesn't seem quite so important.
Mark: So you'd miss the city.
Anna: I'd miss being able to see people without planning it a week in advance. That's what worries me most, not the driving.
Mark: OK, what if we rented somewhere out there for a few months first? See how we feel after a winter.
Anna: That's more like it. If I still like it in February, I'll start looking at houses with you.
Mark: Deal. I'll start looking at rentals tonight.

questions.q: Why is Mark keen on the house?
options: It's right next to a train station
It's bigger and cheaper than their flat
It's close to Anna's office in the town centre
It's near Anna's family and friends
questions.explain_ru: Три спальни, большой сад, и стоит дешевле их квартиры.

questions.q: How often would Mark need to go into the office?
options: Once a week
Three days a week
Every day
Twice a month
questions.explain_ru: Mark: «I'd only have to go into the office once a week». Три дня в неделю — это Anna.

questions.q: Why does Anna know how lovely village life can be?
options: She has friends who live in that village
She grew up in a village herself
She spent last summer in the countryside
She used to work in a village school
questions.explain_ru: «I grew up in a village, so I know how lovely it can be».

questions.q: What worries Anna most about moving?
options: Driving to work three days a week
Paying for such a big house
Feeling cut off from her friends
Having to look after a dog
questions.explain_ru: Больше всего её пугает, что с друзьями нельзя будет видеться без планирования.

questions.q: What does Anna suggest when she mentions it getting dark at four o'clock?
options: Village life can feel lonely in winter
She doesn't enjoy working in the garden
She usually finishes work at four
Shops in villages close very early
questions.explain_ru: Зимой рано темнеет, друзья далеко — в деревне может быть одиноко.

questions.q: What do they decide to do?
options: Buy the house before someone else does
Stay in the city and forget the whole idea
Move closer to Anna's parents in the countryside
Rent a place in the countryside first
questions.explain_ru: Сначала снять жильё за городом на несколько месяцев.

situation_en: A couple are discussing whether to move from the city to the countryside.

topic_en: Interview with a chef about food waste
topic_ru: Интервью с шеф-поваром о пищевых отходах
title: Wasting less food
situation_ru: Ведущая берёт интервью у шеф-повара о том, как меньше выбрасывать еды дома.
script:
Kim: Today I'm talking to Marcus Bell, a chef who's become something of an expert on food waste. Marcus, how much food do we actually throw away?
Marcus: In the average home, it's around a third of what we buy. Which is crazy when you think about it. It's like walking out of the supermarket with three bags and leaving one in the parking lot.
Kim: Why do we waste so much?
Marcus: Mostly because we shop without a plan. We buy for the person we'd like to be, someone who cooks fresh vegetables every night, rather than the person we actually are, who gets home tired and orders pizza.
Kim: That sounds very familiar. So what's your advice?
Marcus: Three things. First, before you shop, look in your fridge and plan four or five meals, not seven. Life always gets in the way. Second, learn to love your freezer. Bread, cooked rice, even milk can be frozen. And third, don't trust best-before dates too much.
Kim: Really? Isn't that risky?
Marcus: There's a difference between best-before and use-by dates. Use-by dates are about safety, and you should take them seriously, especially with meat and fish. Best-before dates are about quality. A yogurt two days past its best-before date is usually perfectly fine. Use your eyes and your nose.
Kim: And what about leftovers?
Marcus: That's my favorite part! In restaurants, we never think of them as leftovers. They're ingredients for tomorrow. Yesterday's roast vegetables become today's soup. Honestly, some of my best dishes started that way.
Kim: Marcus, thank you.

questions.q: How much food does the average home throw away, according to Marcus?
options: Around half of what it buys
About one bag every week
Around a third of what it buys
Around a quarter of what it buys
questions.explain_ru: «In the average home, it's around a third of what we buy».

questions.q: According to Marcus, why do people buy too much food?
options: Supermarkets offer too many special discounts
They shop for the life they wish they had
Their fridges are usually too small
Food goes bad faster than it used to
questions.explain_ru: Мы покупаем для человека, которым хотим быть, а не которым являемся.

questions.q: What does Marcus recommend about planning meals?
options: Plan meals for exactly seven days
Go shopping every single day
Plan four or five meals, not seven
Avoid buying any frozen food
questions.explain_ru: Планировать четыре-пять блюд, а не семь: жизнь вносит коррективы.

questions.q: What does Marcus say about best-before dates?
options: They are mainly about keeping food safe
Food should be thrown away right after them
They only really matter for meat and fish
Food is often still fine after them
questions.explain_ru: Best-before — о качестве, продукт часто ещё вполне хорош.

questions.q: What does Marcus say about use-by dates?
options: They matter much less than best-before dates do
They're mainly about how good the food tastes
You can usually ignore them by two or three days
They're about safety, so take them seriously
questions.explain_ru: «Use-by dates are about safety, and you should take them seriously».

questions.q: How does Marcus feel about leftovers?
options: Excited, because they're ingredients for new dishes
Unsure, because they can be unsafe
Bored, because they always taste the same
Annoyed, because customers in restaurants rarely eat them
questions.explain_ru: Это его любимая часть: остатки — ингредиенты для завтрашних блюд.

situation_en: A presenter interviews a chef about wasting less food at home.
